The fourth presentation on my list is on the leveraging earth observation and AI for scalable climate risk management. by the representative of Luxembourg. Okay, Luxembourg, the floor is yours.

Good afternoon, and thank you for the opportunity to present today. In this presentation, I will show how Earth observation space assets can support the disaster risk management cycle from long-term risk monitoring to post-disaster recovery. I will focus on concrete use cases related to climate and environmental risks, with examples in wildfire, flood and urban heat risk. I will briefly introduce how VEOS technology enhances the value of satellite data for decision makers. Disaster risk does not start at the moment of impact. It is the result of long-term environmental trends, land use change and climate pressures that accumulate over time. The disaster risk management cycle includes planning, preparedness, response and recovery, and satellite data plays a role across all four phases of the cycle. During planning and preparedness, Earth observation allows us to systematically monitor environmental trends at scale. This includes changes in vegetation health, surface temperature, soil moisture and hydrological patterns, all of which are critical indicators for future risk and support hazard mapping and exposure analysis. In response, Earth observation enables rapid situational awareness and damage assessment. And in recovery, it helps track environmental regeneration and effectiveness of interventions over time. The key advantage of Earth observation is consistency. The same data sources can be used before, during and after events, enabling comparability and accountability. By observing environmental variables continuously, VEO supports the planning and preparedness phases in the disaster risk management cycle by offering consistent, high quality Earth observation data that allows anticipation of hazards before they escalate, integration of environmental intelligence into national and regional disaster management plans, and strengthening resilience through informed data-driven preparedness strategies. I will now walk you through three examples of disaster risk assessments used for the planning and preparedness phases. Wildfire risk is not only about fire occurrence but also about exposure and vulnerability. Using Earth observation we can identify areas where vegetation type, density and dryness create high flammability. By combining this with information on the proximity of buildings and infrastructure, it becomes possible to identify properties and assets at elevated risk. This supports the generation of early warnings, but also long-term mitigation strategies, such as vegetation management or land use planning adjustments. Urban heat is a growing, yet unfortunately often underestimated disaster risk. Earth observation allows us to map surface temperature patterns and the potential of neighborhoods to cool down at night, understanding the neighborhoods at risk for the population that lives within. In identified neighborhoods, the tracking of sealed surfaces, roof materials, and potential for cooling infrastructure such as green roofs can be tracked and evaluated. This makes it possible to identify heat hotspots, assess exposure of vulnerable populations, and evaluate whether development is aligned with climate resilient urban planning principles. Similarly, fluvial flood risk is strongly influenced by land use change. Satellite data helps track new impermeable areas and detect potential breaches in development regulations, especially in flood prone zones. This supports enforcement, but also helps planners understand how cumulative urban growth affects runoff and fluvial flood dynamics. a key input for resilient infrastructure planning. One of the limitations associated with openly available satellite data remains spatial resolution, especially linked to urban areas and risk prevention along assets. VEOS technology focuses on improving the effective resolution of satellite imagery, unlocking insights that were previously unavailable. Here you can see a Sentinel-3 thermal imagery at original resolution. With VioTech, we enhance this to Sentinel-2 10 meter resolution, or even more, to extract information closer to the scale at which urban and environmental processes actually occur without requiring entirely new satellite missions. This increases the operational value of existing space assets. Thanks to the resolution enhancement, we derived the following indicators: urban heat retention, flood and wildfire risk, vegetation risk and ecosystem health, nature-based solutions, and integration of lived experience with satellite-derived indicators. This last point is particularly important. Earth observation is most impactful when combined with local knowledge and stakeholder input. VEO integrates all indicators into an accessible digital platform enabling regular satellite-based monitoring of key risk drivers. This includes monitoring of river basins and floodplain areas, heat retention and cool areas, and vegetation stress and connectivity relevant for wildfire risk. The indicators are particularly valuable in regions where ground-based monitoring is limited or uneven, as they allow authorities to prioritize resources and anticipate cascading risks. Beyond alerts, the platform supports risk mitigation. Therefore, VEO provides actionable solutions for authorities and local communities, tailored to the local legal framework, existing mitigation plans, and risk assessments. Finally, it is important to acknowledge that satellite-based disaster risk management has limitations. Local knowledge and expertise are indispensable. For this reason, VEO integrates local communities and practitioners by allowing direct commenting and feedback within the platform. These inputs are processed to support and refine the proposed solutions, as well as to revise and correct risk assessments derived from satellite imagery. VEO considers this inclusion of local expertise crucial for a holistic disaster risk management approach, ensuring that satellite-based insights remain grounded in real-world conditions and lived experience. Veo was founded in 2020 with the objective of taking cutting-edge Earth observation research into real-world applications. The company brings together expertise in remote sensing, environmental engineering, and applied machine learning, with a strong focus on supporting public authorities in climate adaptation and disaster risk management. Our work is grounded in scientific methods but designed to be operational and decision-relevant. To conclude, Earth observation space assets offer unique opportunity to support disaster risk management in a systematic, scalable and transparent way. By improving how we extract and interpret information from existing satellite data, we can better support prevention, preparedness, response and recovery, making crucial information accessible and ultimately reducing human and environmental losses. Thank you for your attention and I look forward to further discussions. Have a great day.
